I liked this game a lot more than I thought I would. really interesting, unlike anything I've ever seen before. pretend to be a hacker without actually knowing anything about programming!

General bugs:
This game was moderately interesting, though buggy, for the first hour or so.  The keyboard didn't always work, so I couldn't type commands at a rate I was used to.  Every once in a while, the keyboard would completely break (you type in a few characters of a command, and the game backspaces them out).  However, you could always save, quit the game, and restart to fix it (although the keyboard was always buggy).  This was on Mac.  I decided to switch to a Windows machine, and the keyboard worked perfectly.

Annoyances:
Commands don't work like you'd think.  Many of them are close to real commands (e.g. scp).  However, you can't download a file to a different filename, like real scp.  AFAICT, there is no way to create a directory.  For someone who likes organization, being only able to put dozens of random files from different missions into one big directory (or move them into one of two subdirectories already created) was frustrating.

Game-breaking bug:
Before I switched platforms, I hit a game-breaking bug on a certain mission where I had to decrypt a file.  My research told me what the password should be, but the command didn't accept the password.  The problem persisted on Windows once I switched.  I spent hours trying to figure out my issue, but failed.  I even did cryptanalysis and found the 'passcode' that was used in encryption, but that did me no good since you cannot type in a passcode.  You must enter the password, which gets converted into the passcode.  With the passcode, I could literally decrypt the file by hand, if only I had a text editor.  A hacker without a text editor?

Ultimately, to my shame, I had to look in the forums, guides, etc.  To my surprise, I found at least 3 different ways that other players solved this mission.  One solved it without a password at all.  Another used the password that I was trying all along.  The third used a misspelling of the name (with a 'd' instead of a 't'), and for some reason it worked.  None of those worked for me.

I have a feeling if I started a new game on Windows, the problem would go away, but I'm not sure if this game is interesting enough to start it all over again.

Review:
The game is interesting, and there are plenty of fun tidbits, such as IRC logs with humorous situations.  They are repetitive, but worth a laugh.  I'm not sure why the executive at KFC spends time on IRC, but whatever. ;)  The missions, though, are very repetitive.  Hack these ports, download a file.  Can't hack a port?  Download some command to do it.  There is no hacking so much as using tools.  You are a script kiddie.  I'm not sure I'd play it again, given the possibility of another game-breaking bug, but I was entertained before that happened (even with the other bugs).

Edit:  I ended up restarting the game on Windows, and all of the bugs described above were fixed, including the game-ender.  I ended up having fun, since I was able to get past the previously completed missions very quickly, and didn't need to nose around the IRC logs, etc. as much as the first play.

Hacknet is a terminal based hacking simulator- Think something along the lines of uplink, but a little more realistic. The game uses UI's similar to that of UNIX and LINUX based interfaces, with the command line being one of your biggest friends in this game. You start the game off small, breaking into weak computers and advancing the story. As time progresses, you become part of a Hacker group and get access to stronger tools. You have to build up stronger resources, hack into firewalls, work fast against traces on your machine, and in the end work towards finding out the death of the mysterious hacker "Bit", and foil the intentions of his killers. The game is short, but does have some community members who are piecing apart the game to make mods. With the game receiving localisations and soon to be receiving a DLC, as well as free modding and multiplayer support, the game does have a future ahead of itself, and should possibly be picked up while at as low of a price as it is now, as you will definitely receive every single cents worth if you are a enthusiast/fan of hacking culture/games.

Hacknet is a semi-realistic terminal-based hacking simulator with scintallating entertainment potential.

You play as an individual who carries out requests that were given to him/her by a recently deceased hacker that went by the psuedonym of "Bit", as well as many other individuals and organizations. These requests typically include breaching servers in order to collect information, deleting logs, rendering services unusable, and various other unscrupulous activities.

Gameplay - 8/10 - When I first began playing Hacknet, I was genuinely surprised at just how realistic and immersive it was. You don't start the game as an omnipotent l337 haxx0r. Your skillset grows over time, and so does your toolset. Tools such as "SSHcrack.exe", "FTPBounce.exe" and others are all realistic in that these could easily be batch files and scripts that a person with malicious intent could use. New tools and gameplay elements are introduced incrementally over time, but even then, it becomes repetitive, and to an extent, stale. 

Soundtrack - 9/10 - The soundtrack primarily consists of electronic music, with a focus on tech house and ambient/chillout. A new song plays for every single stage of the game that you enter, and a new tune plays when you begin a mission. The production value is excellent, and consistent throughout every single track. 

Storyline - ??? - The quality of the storyline is completely subjective and dependent upon the outlook of the player. It may be cringy and cliché to some, yet tantalizing and immersive to others. I can't say much in the way of it without risk of spoiling plot details, but it's Russian Roulette in terms of enjoyability.

Replay Value - 0/10 - No. Stop. No. Stop this right now.

I went into this game with expectations to see something like [url=http://store.steampowered.com/app/383690]MU Complex[/url]; reading tons of e-mails, picking up hints, figuring out stuff on my own, but Hacknet is something different, you get stuff by breaking into other computers and getting it plain and straight ("Password is kingofthesquirrels", "Connect to 64.71.2.102", "Delete this file", "Edit that file") You can still read emails though, it's just not the same.

There are no puzzles as you probably imagine them, more like "Here are five keys, now use them to unlock that box in front of you." type of thing. But nobody tells you that there might be another box behind you that holds the real key to the box. Or that you're supposed to put two keys together and only then try the lock. Or that in the box is a smaller box with more keys. Or that there is a map to the real box inside. Maybe two boxes? And what if, when you finally open it, it's empty?

The main controller is keyboard and you should really try to use only the keyboard as there are points of the game where you just can't use the mouse at all. On the other hand, using the mouse is so much more comfortable for certain actions. I'd recommend getting yourself a third hand.

As for difficulty, it's not hard to learn basic commands by hard and for the others, there's "help" command so I believe anyone can finish this. Also, there's really no way to "lose" the game (at least I didn't find any and I let myself be caught many times in a row), you can always recover and continue.

The storyline is okay, even though most of the time you're kinda wandering on your own, completing missions ranging from [spoiler]deleting a file on target pc[/spoiler] to [spoiler]performing euthanization[/spoiler], not really advancing the story in any way. And while Labyrinths do improve that quite a bit, it's still just that, missions and a bit of plot in between to give those missions a meaning. Still, I think it fits the game well, as you are gathering information, tools, and experience during those missions.

Visuals are great and realistic (BSOD is really too real) and bgm awesome, you really get the feeling you're doing something you probably shouldn't, but there are also fast-paced tracks (Oh god. Shit is going down. DO SOMETHING!).

At 10€ you'll spend 7-12 hours on this game (+ 3-4 in Labyrinths), depending on your skill, and get a soundtrack for free in the game files. Considering how unique Hacknet is, it's pretty good and well worth it. Then, a sale is always an option.

Side note: Labyrinth DLC contains its own story and is in no way required to experience Hacknet's beauty.

That's pretty much the main complaint I can see for this product, otherwise it's fantastic.  The developer has attempted a learning curve where you become more competent throughout the game and aside from the atmosphere it forces you to contemplate tougher choices than I was expecting,  

I am completely fine with changing another human's score on an internet point-click flash game, after all it's just numbers, I'm just changing their numbers from large one to small ones, that's fine.

I am less fine when it comes to changing another humans University Grade and potentially losing them their jobs, when the process is effectively the same, large numbers being turned into small ones- why am I not fine with this one but I was fine with the first??

If you want a super realistic terminal style hacking game with a huge number of computing nuances, this isn't the game for you but if you want a game that makes you think about hacking and consequences for digital security and the sheer amount of power and danger networks represent in the modern world, give it a go.

I picked this game up for $5 a few days ago and played it to completion. A good plot, very good, cyberpunk-ish artstyle, an excellent soundtrack, and the best gameplay of anything I've seen in my life. Not to mention, it uses accurate Linux/Unix commands. 

If you can type fast and have a decent understanding of the Linux terminal, or if you're willing to learn, PLEASE PLAY THIS GAME. It is amazing.

A fun hacking sim! As an Uplink vet, I was a bit disappointed in the lack of customizations (no upgrading sys to have more processing power, etc) and that missions weren't randomized enough each playthrough to feel "fresh." That said, with 3 storylines, there's still enough diversity to have some replay value. I also appreciate the sparse nods to Uplink within the game.

For those that haven't played hacking sims before, I think this is an excellent title to try out. It has a smooth playstyle and nice visuals to accompany it. Give it a shot!
